agent_notes: Verified this is a behavior-preserving refactor: traced each of the five call sites against the pre-diff code. unquote() still runs before _check_path_safe() in all cases (controller.py:92-96), and guard=True is passed only for EXTRACT, DELETE_LOCAL, DELETE_REMOTE (controller.py:123-144), exactly matching which handlers called _check_path_safe before the change. QUEUE and STOP keep guard defaulting to False, matching their pre-diff behavior (they never called _check_path_safe either) — confirmed by checking src/python/controller/controller.py:1122-1126, where QUEUE/STOP are handled without resolving file_name against a local filesystem path the way EXTRACT/DELETE_* do via _check_path_safe. No new injection, auth, or traversal exposure is introduced by this refactor.

Non-blocking maintainability note (not a current vulnerability): _dispatch_command's `guard: bool = False` keyword defaults to the unsafe/unguarded state. If a future destructive action handler is wired through this helper and the author forgets to pass guard=True, it would silently skip the path-safety check. All five current call sites correctly set the flag, so there is no demonstrated bypass today — flagging only as a fail-open-by-default design choice worth a comment or a safer default (e.g. guard required as a positional/keyword with no default, or inferred from an action allowlist like _GUARDED_ACTIONS which already exists at controller.py:159-163 and could be the single source of truth instead of a per-call-site boolean).

The refactor matches ARCH-03 / 108-02-PLAN.md exactly: the signature `_dispatch_command(action, file_name, success_msg, *, guard=False)` is as specified; guard=True is passed for extract/delete_local/delete_remote and omitted for queue/stop; `_process_bulk_commands` is untouched, as the D-03 descope requires.

Behavior is preserved. unquote still runs before the guard, the timeout body is still 'Operation timed out' with status 504, success bodies match the old format strings exactly, and failure still maps to callback.error/error_code. The `if/else` collapsing into an early return does not change semantics.

Naming fits the class's convention: helpers called internally or from tests use a single underscore (`_check_path_safe`, `_process_bulk_commands`), and route handlers use double-underscore name mangling. The tests call `_ControllerHandler__handle_action_*`, and those names still resolve.

The diff adds no new imports, module coupling or dependencies. `Controller.Command.Action` is quoted as a forward-reference annotation, but `_process_bulk_commands` uses the same type unquoted, so the quotes are unnecessary but harmless.

The bulk loop still duplicates the build-command/add-callback/queue_command sequence (lines 349-352). That gives two copies, below the rule of three, and the duplication is explicitly deferred by D-03. Not a finding.

findings.problem: The class already declares which actions need the path-traversal guard in `_GUARDED_ACTIONS` (controller.py:159-163), and the bulk path reads that set (`if action in self._GUARDED_ACTIONS`, line 337). The new `_dispatch_command` ignores the set and takes a caller-supplied `guard: bool = False` instead. That leaves two places that define the same security policy. If a future destructive action is added to `_GUARDED_ACTIONS`, its single-action endpoint is left unguarded unless the author also remembers to pass `guard=True`, and the default is the unsafe setting. The set has only one consumer today, so this falls short of the established-pattern gate (2+ call sites). The plan also explicitly asks for the `guard=` flag.
findings.title: Single-action guard policy is a per-call boolean instead of the class's _GUARDED_ACTIONS set
findings.why_it_matters: This helper decides whether path-traversal protection runs on the destructive endpoints. A default-off flag kept separate from the class-level set can drift silently, and the result would be an unguarded delete or extract.
